acts.lead:
Read the editorial “It’s Time to Modernize Our School Dress Code.” After
reading, carefully analyze the writer’s stand, arguments, and overall
structure. Then, answer the guide questions provided below in complete
sentences. Make sure your answers show your understanding of how
editorial writing presents opinions, supports claims with reasons, and
encourages readers to take action.

It’s Time to Modernize Our School Dress Code
School dress codes are meant to promote discipline and unity, but our
current policy no longer reflects the needs of today’s students. While rules
are important, some parts of the dress code have become outdated,
uncomfortable, and unfair. It is time for the school to update and modernize
the policy to create a more inclusive environment.
First, some of the restrictions no longer match modern clothing trends.
Students are often reprimanded for wearing outfits that are common,
appropriate, and comfortable for everyday use. This not only embarrasses
students but also disrupts their learning. Instead of focusing on small
details like sleeve length or hair accessories, the dress code should focus on
what truly matters: comfort, safety, and respect.
Second, certain rules tend to affect some students more than others.
For example, girls are more frequently disciplined for minor dress code
issues, which can make them feel judged or singled out. A modernized dress
code should be fair and equal, avoiding rules that target specific groups. A
clearer, gender-neutral policy would make the school feel more supportive
for everyone.
Finally, updating the dress code can help students feel more confident.
When students are comfortable with what they wear, they are more likely to
participate in class and stay focused. A simple change in policy can lead to a
more positive school atmosphere.
Updating the dress code doesn’t mean removing rules—it means
improving them. Our school has the chance to create a policy that respects
both tradition and the needs of today’s learners. By revising the dress code,
we can promote fairness, comfort, and confidence for all students. It’s time
to make the change.
Guide Questions:

items.text: What stand or opinion does the writer take about the school dress code, and how is it clearly expressed in the editorial?
What reasons does the writer give to support the claim that the dress code needs to be updated? Identify at least two.
How does the writer show awareness of different perspectives, and why is acknowledging opposing views important in an editorial?
Which part of the editorial serves as the “call to action,” and how does it encourage readers to support change?
How does the structure of the editorial (introduction, body, conclusion) help make the argument clear and persuasive?

items.text: Pick a Social Media Trend or Issue o     Choose a trend, challenge, or issue related to social media that is relevant to teenagers: mental health, “cancel culture,” misinformation, viral challenges, body image, privacy, digital activism, etc.

Research o     Find data, news stories, and real-life examples about your topic. o     Interview at least two people: classmates, teachers, or someone in your community who has an opinion or experience with this trend or issue.

Plan Your Feature o     Use a graphic organizer to outline: ▪   A hook (a surprising fact, a personal story, or a question) ▪   Background / context ▪   Real-life stories / quotes from your interviews ▪   A reflection or call to action: Why should people care? What can be done?

Write Your Feature Article o     Write a 5-paragraph feature: ▪   Lead: Start with an anecdote or fact related to the trend ▪   Body 1: Explain the trend / issue (what it is, how it started) ▪   Body 2: Share stories or impact (quotes from interviews) ▪   Body 3: Discuss positive and negative effects / complexities ▪   Conclusion: Reflect on what the trend means for you and your peers propose a solution, raise a question, or call to action. Example: Title: The Invisible Weight: Social Media and Teen Mental Health Lead (Paragraph 1): Every night around 10 PM, 15-year-old Kayla opens TikTok, swipes through a stream of dance videos, beauty tutorials, and vloggers talking about their “glow-up” journeys. She pauses on a clip where a popular creator talks about how they feel “not good enough” without filters. “Sometimes I feel like that too,” Kayla says quietly. For many teenagers, the glow of their phone screen doesn’t just light up their room — it also lights up insecurities. Body 1 (Explaining the Trend): social media plays a huge role in teenage life today. According to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey, 45% of teens say they spend too much time on social media — a number that’s risen steadily in recent years. While many teens say these platforms help them feel more connected (74%) or creative (63%), others admit there’s a cost: nearly 1 in 5 say social media hurts their mental health. At the same time, a World Health Organization report found that about 11% of adolescents show signs of problematic social media use — struggling to control their usage and feeling negative consequences. Body 2 (Stories & Impact): To understand how this plays out in real life, I spoke with two classmates, Marco and Jess. Marco, 16, says his TikTok notifications are a “double- edged sword.” “When I get a lot of likes I feel proud, but when I don’t, I question why I even posted,” he says. Jess, 14, says Instagram is a place for both connection and competition. “I follow people who seem to have perfect lives — but when I compare, I feel small,” she admits. Their experiences reflect a bigger pattern: that behind every “like” or share is often a struggle with self-worth. Body 3 (Complexities — Positives & Negatives): social media isn’t all bad. Many teens use it as a place for self-expression, community, and even healing. In the same Pew survey, 34% of teens said they sometimes get mental health information from these platforms — and of those, 63% say it’s an important source. But the negatives are real, too. According to the Mayo Clinic, what teens do on social media matters: viewing content about self-harm, unrealistic beauty standards, or risky behavior can increase anxiety and low self-esteem. Experts suggest that moderation may be key — because using social media doesn’t necessarily have to be harmful, but overuse or exposure to certain content can be. Conclusion (Reflection / Call to Action): So what can we, as teens, do about this? First, we can set healthier boundaries — limit screen time, mute stressful accounts, and take “digital detox” breaks. Second, we can support each other: talk openly when we feel the pressure of comparison or when social media messes with our self- esteem. And finally, we can push for a change: schools can host workshops about healthy social media habits, and we can encourage creators to show real life — not just the highlight reel. If we learn to use social media with purpose, maybe we can make it a place that builds us up — instead of weighing us down.

Write Your Draft Write a 4- or 5-paragraph feature article: ▪   Paragraph 1 (Lead): Open with a scene, personal story, or fact that highlights the environmental issue. ▪   Paragraph 2: Explain what the problem is, with data / background. ▪   Paragraph 3: Include voices from your interviews — real people, quotes, personal impact. ▪   Paragraph 4: Describe current efforts or possible solutions. ▪   Paragraph 5 (Conclusion): Reflect on why this issue matters and suggest a call-to-action or hope for change. Example: Title: Sachets, Streets, and the Sea: How Plastic Pollution Affects Our Community Paragraph 1 (Lead): On a typical morning, 14-year-old Mia walks beside the small creek that winds behind her neighborhood. She used to toss snack wrappers and empty sachet packets on the ground — “they’re small,” she would say, “they’ll just disappear.” But now, she pauses. The creek is no longer clear: she sees bits of colorful plastic bobbing on the surface. “When I was younger, I never thought my trash could end up in the sea,” she admits. Paragraph 2 (Background / Problem): Plastic pollution is a massive problem in the Philippines. According to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), about 24% of the country’s daily 61,000 metric tons of solid waste is plastic. Every year, the Philippines generates around 2.7 million metric tons of plastic waste, much of which ends up in landfills, rivers, or the ocean. Single-use plastics, like sachets, are especially problematic — they don’t biodegrade, they break down into microplastics, and they contribute to flooding by clogging drainage systems. Paragraph 3 (Voices / Stories): I spoke with Mr. Navarro, a barangay (village) official, who says, “Plastic waste isn’t just dirty — it’s dangerous.” He explained that clogged waterways during the rainy season make flooding worse, especially when heavy rains come. I also met Marisol; a local youth volunteer who helps organize barangay cleanups. “We collect plastic sachets every weekend,” she told me. “It’s heartbreaking to see how many people don’t bother to put trash in bins.” Paragraph 4 (Solutions / Efforts): There are hopeful signs. In 2025, the government launched the National Plastic Action Partnership (NPAP) to address plastic waste with stronger collaboration among communities, businesses, and government agencies. At the local level, students in Mia’s school started a “Plastic to Purpose” drive: they collect used sachets, sort them, and send them to a recycling center. For the microplastics that don’t get recycled, they’re talking to barangay officials about installing filters in the creek to trap litter before it reaches the sea. But she also knows that change isn’t just on her shoulders. We — as a school and a community — need to act. We can reduce single-use plastics, support local cleanups, and pressure companies to package products responsibly. If enough of us do something, maybe one day, the creek won’t be plastic-filled, and our streets won’t feed our seas.
